themes.thesis: The most predictable demand curve available: the population that consumes the most healthcare is already born and already counted. What is uncertain is not the demand but who is paid for meeting it, since the same demographics that create the volume also strain the payers - so this theme is scoped to the companies that supply care capacity rather than the insurers who bear its cost.

chain.root_driver: The over-65 share of the population rises for another two decades in every developed market, and healthcare consumption per person rises steeply with age while the clinical workforce does not grow with it.
chain.first_order: Procedure volume: the device makers, orthopedic and cardiovascular implants, and the facilities where those procedures happen.
chain.second_order: Diagnostics and imaging that route patients into procedures, the consumables and sterilization behind each one, and the software that lets a constrained workforce carry more volume per clinician.
chain.disconfirming: Procedure volume growth normalizing after the post-pandemic catch-up rather than continuing; reimbursement rates cut faster than volume grows; hospital capital budgets tightening; staffing shortages capping throughput regardless of demand.

themes.thesis: A multi-year capex cycle in AI compute pulls through demand for accelerators, HBM/DRAM/NAND memory, networking silicon, and grid and data-center power. The exposure worth identifying is upstream of the spending, not downstream of the share price that has already responded to it.

chain.root_driver: Training and serving large models turns compute into a capital expenditure rather than a software cost, so a handful of buyers commit multi-year budgets to buildings, silicon and power ahead of the revenue those models earn.
chain.first_order: Accelerators, high-bandwidth memory and the networking silicon that lashes them together - the parts of the spend specified by the model rather than by the building.
chain.second_order: Everything the building needs before a chip can run in it: power distribution and conversion, thermal management, the contractors who build the halls, and the generation and grid capacity that has to exist first.
chain.disconfirming: Hyperscaler capex guidance cut or deferred; memory pricing rolling over on oversupply rather than demand; equipment lead times shortening; the buildout concentrating in a single customer whose own spending is slowing.

themes.thesis: The cleanest structural chain that owes nothing to AI enthusiasm: labor is scarce and expensive in exactly the places manufacturing and logistics are being rebuilt, and the substitution is bought as equipment rather than hired. What makes it durable is that the payback is arithmetic - a wage bill against a machine price - so the spending survives the sentiment cycle that thematic screens usually mistake for a trend.

chain.root_driver: Working-age population growth has stalled in every large manufacturing economy while wages in warehousing and assembly keep rising, so output per worker has to come from capital rather than headcount.
chain.first_order: Robots, motion control and machine vision - the equipment that directly replaces a task, bought against a payback period rather than a forecast.
chain.second_order: The sensors, drives, controllers and precision components inside those machines, the industrial software that schedules them, and the integrators who install them.
chain.disconfirming: Machine tool and robot order books turning down; wage growth in logistics and assembly decelerating, which removes the payback; capex guidance from automotive and warehousing customers being cut; integrators reporting project deferrals rather than backlog.

themes.thesis: A battery storage backlog is a contracted interconnection commitment, not an announcement - which is why this theme weights order backlog more heavily than most others in the screen: it is the most direct evidence that a project has cleared the queue rather than merely entered it.

chain.root_driver: Grid-scale storage is the buffer that lets intermittent generation and firm demand clear the same interconnection queue as thermal and nuclear capacity, so it is funded by the same load-growth pressure driving the rest of the electrification buildout rather than by climate policy alone.
chain.first_order: Utility-scale battery energy storage system integrators, whose order backlog is the earliest evidence of contracted, not merely announced, storage capacity.
chain.second_order: The power-electronics and enclosure suppliers into those systems, and the regulated utilities whose capital plans and interconnection agreements fund the buildout.
chain.disconfirming: Interconnection queues clearing faster than new storage requests arrive; utility storage procurement targets missed rather than raised; backlog-to-revenue conversion stalling while backlog itself keeps growing, the same warning this screen watches for in other themes.

themes.thesis: This buildout has failed before on the same mechanism every time: a dominant producer undercuts new domestic capacity on price before it reaches scale. What is different this round is that offtake and price-floor agreements are increasingly government-backed rather than spot-price bets, which is why contracted volume and named-customer evidence matter more here than for most themes in this screen.

chain.root_driver: A small number of countries control rare-earth and critical-mineral processing, and export controls on that processing have turned magnet and battery-metal supply into a national- security question with a multi-year, government-backed response rather than a commodity cycle that clears on price alone.
chain.first_order: Domestic and allied miners and separators of rare earths and battery-relevant minerals, increasingly funded by government offtake and price-floor agreements rather than spot pricing alone.
chain.second_order: The magnet, alloy and specialty-chemical processors who turn separated material into a usable input, and the defense and electrification buyers whose named contracts anchor it.
chain.disconfirming: Offtake and price-floor agreements not renewed at expiration; export controls easing rather than tightening; a dominant producer flooding the spot market to undercut new domestic capacity, the tactic that has repeatedly ended prior attempts at this buildout.

themes.thesis: The supplier theme that every other digital theme feeds: each new workload, payment rail and connected device widens the surface someone has to defend, and the budget is non-discretionary in a way most software spending is not. It is also the theme where filing language is least trustworthy - every company on earth writes about protecting its own data - so the keyword list is written to catch vendors and the exclusions to reject the far larger population describing its own risk.

chain.root_driver: Attack surface grows mechanically with cloud adoption, remote access, digital payments and connected devices, while regulation increasingly makes disclosure and control a legal obligation rather than a technical preference.
chain.first_order: The platform vendors: identity, endpoint, network and cloud security sold as recurring subscriptions.
chain.second_order: The consultancies and managed providers who operate it for firms without a security team, and the network and appliance makers whose hardware enforces it.
chain.disconfirming: Net revenue retention falling as customers consolidate onto fewer platforms; billings growth decelerating faster than revenue; enterprise security budgets being folded into a shrinking overall IT line; breach disclosures no longer producing budget responses.

themes.thesis: Liquid cooling changed from an option to a rack-density specification, which makes attach rate the thing worth measuring rather than the presence of a "cooling" segment: a vendor with a legacy air-cooling or automotive-thermal business looks similar on a keyword screen to one whose growth is entirely in liquid cooling for accelerators, and only segment and backlog evidence tells them apart.

chain.root_driver: Accelerator rack density has moved past what air cooling can remove, so liquid cooling has gone from an option to a specification for the newest accelerator generations - a physical constraint on the AI buildout, not a preference.
chain.first_order: The thermal-management and power-quality vendors data-center operators specify directly: liquid cooling loops, coolant distribution units, and the power gear that shares the rack.
chain.second_order: Heat-exchange and thermal component suppliers, and the contractors who retrofit or build halls to the new cooling specification.
chain.disconfirming: Accelerator generations reverting to air-cooled designs; hyperscaler cooling capex guidance cut; liquid-cooling attach rates flattening in disclosed data-center wins; a shift to lower-density inference-only buildouts that do not need it.

themes.thesis: Cash displacement is a decades-long substitution that compounds quietly: every transaction that moves onto a card or an account-to-account rail becomes a metered event for the network carrying it. The economics belong to the toll collectors rather than the banks, which is why this theme is scoped to networks, processors and software rather than to lenders whose earnings turn on credit and rates.

chain.root_driver: Cash and cheque volume keeps converting to electronic payment, and commerce, payroll and billing increasingly embed a payment step inside software rather than beside it.
chain.first_order: The networks and processors that clear the transaction and price it per event.
chain.second_order: Fraud, identity and risk systems that make the rails usable at scale; the core banking and issuer-processing software beneath them; and the terminal and hardware makers at the point of sale.
chain.disconfirming: Payment volume growth converging on nominal consumption growth, which means the substitution is finished; take rates compressing under regulatory caps or account-to- account rails that bypass the networks; consumer credit deteriorating enough to shrink transaction volume itself.

themes.thesis: Reliability and sovereignty have displaced cost as the first question asked of an energy system. That favors what can be dispatched on demand and sourced domestically - gas infrastructure, LNG export, nuclear - and it is a different bet from the decarbonization theme it is routinely confused with, which is why the two are not merged here.

chain.root_driver: Governments and large buyers now price the risk of an interrupted or foreign-controlled supply, and simultaneous load growth means firm, dispatchable capacity is scarce for the first time in a generation.
chain.first_order: The producers and generators themselves: gas and oil operators, independent power producers, and nuclear operators selling into long-dated contracts.
chain.second_order: Pipelines, liquefaction and storage; the drilling, completion and equipment supply chain; turbines and reactor components; and the fuel cycle behind them.
chain.disconfirming: Long-dated LNG offtake contracts failing to renew; permitting reform stalling; power prices falling on new supply rather than weak demand; capital discipline breaking down into a drilling boom, which historically ends this trade rather than extends it.
